Primary paradigm: dp
Specific paradigm: digit_dp_for_forbidden_digits
Algorithm template: dynamic_programming
Solution models: sequence_dp, counting_combinatorics
Main object: integers in an interval and whether their decimal representation contains 4 or 9
Main condition: count forbidden numbers in [A, B] as f(B) - f(A - 1)
Structural property: the prefix relation to x and the seen-forbidden flag determine all remaining choices
Update or transition: process digits from most significant to least significant and update tight and forbidden states
Answer extraction: subtract the prefix count below A from the prefix count up to B
Template-specific: answer_extraction: f(x) is the sum of terminal states with seen = true; base_cases: dp[0][true][false] = 1; iteration_order: from the most significant digit to the least significant digit; state_definition: dp[pos][tight][seen] counts prefixes of length pos, where seen records whether digit 4 or 9 has appeared; transition: append a digit within the tight bound, update tight, and set seen if the digit is 4 or 9
Core computations: forbidden_digit_transition = next_seen = seen || digit == 4 || digit == 9 (records exactly when a candidate number becomes forbidden); interval_count = answer = f(B) - f(A - 1) (turns prefix counting into the requested closed interval count)
Complexity: O(D), where D is number of decimal digits of B

Primary paradigm: greedy
Specific paradigm: lexicographically_smallest_permutation_under_mismatch_budget
Algorithm template: greedy
Solution models: global_invariant_greedy
Main object: a permutation t of S with at most K positions different from S
Main condition: a partial prefix is feasible when the current mismatches plus the minimum necessary suffix mismatches do not exceed K
Structural property: after fixing a prefix, suffix feasibility depends only on remaining character supplies and demands
Update or transition: try candidate characters in lexicographic order and commit the first feasible one
Answer extraction: the greedily built string is the lexicographically smallest feasible permutation
Template-specific: exchange_argument: if a smaller candidate passes the suffix mismatch lower bound, replacing the current position by it cannot make the remaining multiset infeasible; greedy_choice: place the smallest remaining character whose prefix can still be completed within K mismatches; invariant: the fixed prefix is lexicographically minimum among all feasible prefixes of the same length; sorting_key: increasing character order at each position
Core computations: suffix_mismatch_lower_bound = need = sum_sigma max(demand_sigma, supply_sigma) (tests whether the unfinished suffix can be arranged within the remaining mismatch budget); candidate_feasibility = fixed_mismatches + (candidate != S[i]) + need <= K (decides whether a lexicographic candidate can be committed)
Complexity: O(N * |Sigma|), where N is length of the string, |Sigma| is alphabet size

Primary paradigm: dp
Specific paradigm: grid_diamond_erosion_dp
Algorithm template: dynamic_programming
Solution models: precomputed_lookup, grid_graph_traversal
Main object: grid cells that can be centers of an all-o diamond of radius K
Main condition: a cell survives one expansion step only if the cell and its four neighbors survived the previous step
Structural property: K - 1 repeated local erosions leave exactly the valid diamond centers
Update or transition: next[r][c] = prev[r][c] and prev[r-1][c] and prev[r+1][c] and prev[r][c-1] and prev[r][c+1]
Answer extraction: count true cells after K - 1 transitions
Template-specific: answer_extraction: number of cells with ok[K - 1][r][c] = true; base_cases: ok[0][r][c] = true exactly for original o cells; iteration_order: increase step from 0 to K - 1 and scan all grid cells each step; state_definition: ok[step][r][c] is true when every cell within Manhattan distance step from (r, c) is o; transition: ok[step+1][r][c] is the conjunction of ok[step] at (r,c) and its four orthogonal neighbors
Core computations: diamond_erosion_transition = next[r][c] = prev[r][c] && prev[r-1][c] && prev[r+1][c] && prev[r][c-1] && prev[r][c+1] (grows the guaranteed all-o diamond radius by one)
Complexity: O(KHW), where H is grid height, K is required diamond radius, W is grid width

Primary paradigm: greedy
Specific paradigm: robot_move_contribution_sort
Algorithm template: greedy
Solution models: global_invariant_greedy, linear_scan_accumulation
Main object: each M command's contribution coefficient from later plus and minus commands
Main condition: the robot must choose the same number of positive and negative M moves to finish at the origin
Structural property: after fixing the coefficient of every M, the optimal assignment is independent except for choosing half of them positive
Update or transition: scan S from right to left, maintain plus_count - minus_count, and record that balance at each M
Answer extraction: sort the coefficients, subtract the lower half, and add the upper half
Template-specific: exchange_argument: if a positive move has a smaller coefficient than a negative move, swapping their signs increases or preserves the total happiness; greedy_choice: assign negative direction to the smallest coefficients and positive direction to the largest coefficients; invariant: exactly half of the M moves are positive and half negative, so pairing extremes maximizes the signed sum; sorting_key: increasing contribution coefficient of an M move
Core computations: right_side_balance = coef(M_i) = number_of_plus_to_right - number_of_minus_to_right (measures how much choosing the positive direction for that M affects final happiness); optimal_signed_sum = answer = sum(largest half coefficients) - sum(smallest half coefficients) (maximizes happiness under the return-to-origin constraint)
Complexity: O(L log L), where L is length of the command string

Primary paradigm: implementation
Specific paradigm: two_pointer_product_window
Algorithm template: two_pointer
Solution models: two_pointer_window
Main object: contiguous subarrays and their product
Main condition: a window is valid when the product of its elements is at most K
Structural property: with all elements positive, increasing the right endpoint can only increase the product until the left endpoint is advanced
Update or transition: multiply by the new right element, then divide away left elements while the product exceeds K
Answer extraction: track the maximum valid window length
Template-specific: answer_extraction: maximum length recorded among valid windows; key_operations: return N immediately if any element is zero, extend R by multiplying the product, advance L and divide while the product exceeds K, maximize R - L; main_structure: sliding window [L, R) with its current product
Core computations: window_product_update = prod *= S[R]; while prod > K: prod /= S[L]; L += 1 (maintains the longest valid positive-product window ending at R)
Complexity: O(N), where N is sequence length

Primary paradigm: math
Specific paradigm: base_digit_sum_divisor_search
Algorithm template: exhaustive_enumeration
Solution models: math_formula_transformation, exhaustive_enumeration
Main object: base b representation of N and its digit sum
Main condition: if digit_sum_b(N) = S, then b - 1 divides N - S; small bases are checked directly
Structural property: large-base candidates are restricted by the divisor relation N - S = q * (b - 1)
Update or transition: enumerate candidate bases and compute digit sums by repeated division
Answer extraction: take the smallest valid base or -1 if none exists
Template-specific: aggregation: maintain the minimum valid base; answer_extraction: minimum valid base, otherwise -1; candidate_condition: digit_sum_b(N) equals S and b >= 2; enumeration_order: check small bases in increasing order, then enumerate divisors of N - S; pruning: if N = S, answer is N + 1; if N < S, no base can work; search_space: bases b from 2 through sqrt(N), plus bases d + 1 where d divides N - S
Core computations: digit_sum_in_base = while x > 0: sum += x % b; x //= b (checks whether a candidate base realizes the required digit sum); divisor_candidate = b = d + 1 for each divisor d of N - S (uses the editorial divisibility condition to avoid scanning all large bases)
Complexity: O(sqrt(N) log N), where N is given number

Primary paradigm: dp
Specific paradigm: carry_free_xor_sum_recursion
Algorithm template: dynamic_programming
Solution models: sequence_dp, counting_combinatorics
Main object: pairs (u, s) satisfying u + 2s <= N and (u & s) = 0
Main condition: the least significant parity cases reduce the count to three smaller bounds
Structural property: carry-free bit choices are independent after dividing both values by two
Update or transition: F(n) = F(floor(n/2)) + F(floor((n-1)/2)) + F(floor((n-2)/2))
Answer extraction: evaluate F(N) modulo 1,000,000,007
Template-specific: answer_extraction: F(N) modulo 1,000,000,007; base_cases: F(n) = 0 for n < 0, F(0) = 1; iteration_order: memoized recursion on decreasing values of n, or bottom-up over reachable floor-halves; state_definition: F(n) is the number of valid pairs (u, s) with u + 2s <= n and (u & s) = 0; transition: split by the parity of (u, s): (even, even), (odd, even), and (even, odd)
Core computations: parity_split_recurrence = F(n) = F(n/2) + F((n-1)/2) + F((n-2)/2) (counts the three legal low-bit cases without introducing carries)
Complexity: O(log N), where N is upper bound

Primary paradigm: math
Specific paradigm: bounded_three_variable_sum_counting
Algorithm template: counting_accumulation
Solution models: counting_combinatorics, incremental_counting
Main object: triples (x, y, z) with each value in [0, K]
Main condition: for each fixed z, x + y must equal S - z within the bounded square [0, K]^2
Structural property: the number of bounded pairs depends only on the interval of feasible x values
Update or transition: add max(0, min(K, T) - max(0, T - K) + 1) for T = S - z
Answer extraction: sum the pair counts over all z
Template-specific: answer_extraction: total accumulated number of triples; key_operations: fix z from 0 to K, compute T = S - z, count x values satisfying 0 <= x <= K and 0 <= T - x <= K, accumulate the count; main_structure: one-dimensional accumulation over the chosen value z
Core computations: bounded_pair_count = count2(T) = max(0, min(K, T) - max(0, T - K) + 1) (counts valid (x, y) pairs after z is fixed)
Complexity: O(K), where K is upper bound for each variable

Primary paradigm: dp
Specific paradigm: subset_sum_neediness_test
Algorithm template: dynamic_programming
Solution models: sequence_dp, precomputed_lookup
Main object: whether each card is necessary for reaching threshold K
Main condition: card i is necessary iff some subset of the other cards has sum in [K - a_i, K)
Structural property: subset-sum reachability below K is represented by coefficients of product (1 + x^{a_j}) modulo x^K
Update or transition: obtain the excluding-i reachability polynomial as product_{j != i}(1 + x^{a_j}) and inspect the critical interval
Answer extraction: count cards whose excluding-i polynomial has no reachable sum in the critical interval
Template-specific: answer_extraction: card i is counted as no-need when no reachable_i[s] exists for K - a_i <= s < K; base_cases: sum 0 is reachable before using any card; iteration_order: build coefficients for sums below K, then evaluate each card's excluding polynomial; state_definition: reachable_i[s] indicates whether sum s < K is achievable without card i; transition: subset-sum multiplication by (1 + x^{a_j}) modulo x^K; excluding-i states are derived from the all-card product by the editorial division idea
Core computations: necessity_interval = needed(i) = exists s in [K - a_i, K) with [x^s] product_{j != i}(1 + x^{a_j}) != 0 (characterizes exactly when card i can be the final card that reaches K); truncated_subset_sum_product = F(x) = product_j (1 + x^{a_j}) mod x^K (stores all subset sums relevant to the threshold)
Complexity: O(NK), where K is threshold, N is number of cards

Primary paradigm: graph
Specific paradigm: bellman_ford_positive_cycle_score_detection
Algorithm template: graph_traversal
Solution models: state_space_shortest_path, graph_connectivity_under_constraints
Main object: directed weighted graph from vertex 1 to vertex N
Main condition: the answer is infinite exactly when a positive-score cycle is reachable from 1 and can still reach N
Structural property: negating edge scores turns maximum score into shortest path with negative-cycle detection
Update or transition: relax dist[to] with dist[from] - score for Bellman-Ford passes and propagate improvements that can reach N
Answer extraction: output inf if the target is affected by such a cycle; otherwise output -dist[N]
Template-specific: edge_definition: an input edge a -> b with score c becomes relaxation cost -c; graph_model: directed graph with negated edge costs for Bellman-Ford relaxation; node_definition: each original vertex stores a shortest negated distance and an affected-by-negative-cycle flag; traversal_order: N - 1 full edge-relaxation passes, followed by extra passes or reachability filtering for negative-cycle influence; visited_state: dist[v] is finite only when v is reachable from 1; affected[v] is true when an improving cycle can propagate to v
Core computations: bellman_ford_relaxation = dist[b] = min(dist[b], dist[a] - c) (computes the best finite score path after negating scores); infinite_score_condition = exists improving edge after N - 1 passes whose improved vertex can reach N (distinguishes harmless positive cycles from cycles that make the final score unbounded)
Complexity: O(NM), where M is number of directed edges, N is number of vertices

Primary paradigm: graph
Specific paradigm: bridge_count_by_edge_removal
Algorithm template: graph_traversal
Solution models: graph_connectivity_under_constraints
Main object: each undirected edge of the graph
Main condition: an edge is a bridge iff removing it disconnects the graph
Structural property: connectivity after removing a single edge is checked by one DFS or BFS that skips that edge
Update or transition: for each candidate edge, traverse all remaining edges and test whether every vertex is reached
Answer extraction: count the candidate edges whose removal makes some vertex unreachable
Template-specific: edge_definition: all input edges except the currently tested edge; graph_model: undirected graph with one candidate edge temporarily removed; node_definition: original graph vertices; traversal_order: DFS or BFS from vertex 1 for each edge-removal trial; visited_state: visited[v] records whether v remains reachable after the candidate edge is skipped
Core computations: bridge_trial = is_bridge(e) = not all vertices are reachable in G without e (directly implements the definition of a bridge)
Complexity: O(M(N + M)), where M is number of edges, N is number of vertices

Primary paradigm: implementation
Specific paradigm: piecewise_linear_speed_profile_scan
Algorithm template: linear_scan
Solution models: linear_scan_accumulation, prefix_suffix_aggregation
Main object: maximum feasible train speed at each integer time
Main condition: speed is bounded by segment speed limits, start/end zero speed, and acceleration at most 1 per second
Structural property: a forward pass and backward pass enforce all adjacent acceleration constraints
Update or transition: a[k] = min(a[k], segment_cap, a[k-1] + 1, a[k+1] + 1)
Answer extraction: sum the area under the resulting piecewise-linear speed curve
Template-specific: answer_extraction: total area under the feasible maximum speed profile; key_operations: apply each segment's speed cap to all covered integer times and unit intervals, set a[0] and a[M] to zero, scan forward and backward to enforce acceleration limits, accumulate each unit interval's trapezoid or peak area; main_structure: arrays a[0..M] for integer-time speeds and d[0..M-1] for per-second caps
Core computations: forward_backward_speed_cap = a[i] = min(a[i], a[i-1] + 1) and a[i] = min(a[i], a[i+1] + 1) (enforces acceleration and deceleration feasibility); unit_interval_area = area_i = (a[i] + a[i+1]) / 2 if endpoints differ, else a[i] or a[i] + 0.25 depending on the interval cap (adds the exact distance traveled during one second)
Complexity: O(M + N), where M is sum of all segment durations, N is number of speed-limit segments

Primary paradigm: graph
Specific paradigm: residue_graph_shortest_digit_sum
Algorithm template: graph_traversal
Solution models: state_space_shortest_path
Main object: residue of a positive decimal number modulo K
Main condition: appending a digit x moves residue r to (10r + x) mod K with digit-sum cost x
Structural property: the minimum digit sum among multiples of K is a shortest path to residue 0
Update or transition: relax dist[(10r + x) mod K] with dist[r] + x for digits x
Answer extraction: the shortest distance to residue 0
Template-specific: edge_definition: append digit x to transition r -> (10r + x) mod K with cost x; graph_model: directed weighted graph over residues modulo K plus a virtual start; node_definition: residue classes 0 through K - 1; traversal_order: Dijkstra priority order by current digit-sum cost; visited_state: dist[r] is the minimum digit sum of a constructed positive number with residue r
Core computations: append_digit_transition = to = (10 * r + x) % K; cost += x (models decimal construction while preserving only the residue)
Complexity: O(K log K), where K is given divisor

Core computations: shortcut_transition = dp[i][s+i-j-1] = min(dp[i][...], dp[j][s] + hypot(P_i-P_j)) (uses a direct shortcut between visited checkpoints); skip_penalty = penalty(s) = 0 if s=0 else 2^(s-1) (final cost added for skipped checkpoints)
